title: How to Heal a Divided World: Argumentative Writing that Actually Listens to the Other Side ative-writing-that-actually-listens-to-the-other-side
author: Beaton, Erica
source: Dave Stuart Jr. (davestuartjr.com) -- guest post by Erica Beaton, October 7, 2021
summary: Guest author Erica Beaton, writing on Dave Stuart Jr.'s blog about research she conducted with a team of teacher-researchers (Dave included), argues that the standard "win the debate, shoot down the opposition" model of argumentative writing trains students in the same corrosiveness that poisons public discourse. Drawing on her classroom research into a traditional social-issues research paper unit, she proposes an eight-move alternative built around empathy: independent reading as a window into other identities, curating heart-breaking social issues, humanizing the "other side" with a two-column values chart, using the YouTube series Middle Ground as a mentor text, researching from "two heads" (both sides' fears and motivations), an ICEEE structure adapted to expose the other side's values, sentence starters that listen, and a rebuilt rebuttal paragraph that holds the weight of the opposition's belief before diverging or reaching an impasse. She illustrates the approach's effect with two student anecdotes -- a pro-life student who shifted his claim after researching support for pregnant mothers, and a pro-choice student who chose an honest impasse rather than a forced resolution. The piece closes by reframing the goal of argumentative writing from "winning" to "solving a problem," arguing this produces both more mature writing and more capable citizens.
points: The standard argumentative-writing model that trains students to "shoot down" the opposition replicates the corrosive dynamics of political discourse rather than counteracting them.

A two-column "Humanize the Other Side" organizer -- prompting students to ask what kind of people hold the opposing view, what experiences brought them there, and what they value -- forces research beyond a single perspective before drafting begins.

Rebuilding the rebuttal paragraph around holding the weight of the opponent's belief, then explicitly choosing either a Divergence (moving forward while acknowledging the other side) or an Impasse (conceding the divide is unresolved), gives students an honest alternative to false certainty.

Real classroom evidence -- a pro-life student who reworked his claim after discovering how little support exists for pregnant mothers, and a pro-choice student who chose an honest impasse over forced resolution -- shows the method changing students' actual thinking, not just their prose.
quotes: In many places, students are taught a standard model to present their own points and "shoot down" elements of their opposition. While this feels triumphant, especially with a one-reader teacher-audience, it doesn't equip students to communicate in healthy and productive ways.

With a team of teacher researchers -- Dave included -- I spent time the last few years examining the pitfalls of argumentative writing and crafted methods to teach students to use nuance and empathy to achieve productive civil discourse.
Aside from writing that has great potential to solve the political divide of our world (no small feat, right?), essays that practice empathy are more dynamic and interesting to read.

Students need to pivot from just grabbing a quote from each article -- if you've taught research writing for more than a day, you know this is standard practice -- to actually understanding how the message, the audience, and the communicator are perceived by supporters and opponents of their topic.
He wanted to shift his claim from "The government should make abortions illegal" to a more nuanced "The government should support pregnant mothers.

When teaching this step, I physically pulled two chairs together in the front of my classroom and talked to the imaginary person on the other side of my issue. I picked up their invisible, emotional knapsack and held it in my arms, bearing the heaviness of their heart.
We have an opportunity when we teach argumentative writing to turn the opposition back into an actual person. We can teach students to sit right next to their adversary on middle ground.
Not only will this make the writing more mature and dynamic, but -- with empathy and nuance -- our young writers might actually change someone's mind and help heal this divided world.
